'''Norman J. Pullman''' ({{Birth date|1931|3|31}} – {{Date of death|1999|5|28}}) was a mathematician, professor of mathematics, and Doctor of Mathematics, who specialized in [[number theory]], [[matrix theory]], [[linear algebra]], and [[Tournament theory|theory of tournaments]].<ref name=gene>{{MathGenealogy|id=25235}}</ref><ref name= tribute>{{cite book  |title= Graphs, Matrices, and Designs: Festschrift in Honor of Norman J. Pullman|author= Pullman, N.J. |author2= Rees, R.S.|isbn= 9780824787905|lccn= lc92024370|series= Lecture Notes in Pure and Applied Mathematics Series|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=zuZFgYZqmkMC|year= 1993|publisher= CRC Press Inc }}</ref><ref name=bulletin>{{cite journal | author= David A. Gregory |author2 = Stephen J. Kirkland |title= Norman J. Pullman (1931–1999) |issue= 23 |year = 1999 |journal = The Bulletin of the International Linear Algebra Society |publisher = McGill University }}</ref>

==Career==

He earned an M.A. degree in mathematics from [[Harvard University]], and in 1962, he was awarded the Doctorate degree of Mathematics from [[Syracuse University]].
<ref name=tribute/>

From 1962 to 1965, he was professor of Mathematics at [[McGill University]]. And in 1965 he was awarded a postdoctoral fellowship at [[University of Alberta]].<ref name=tribute/>

In 1965 he started to work at the faculty of [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]], and held a professorship position since 1971.<ref name=tribute/>

He lectured in professional meetings for the [[American Mathematical Society]] and the [[Australian Mathematical Society]].

He was a visiting scholar for [[Curtin University|Curtin University of Technology]] in a great many occasions, and had a professional association with the institution.

During his career, he supervised mathematicians like [[Dominique de Caen]], [[Rolf S. Rees]], and [[Bill Jackson (mathematician)|Bill Jackson]], among others.<ref name=tribute/>

His research included contributions in [[matrix theory]], [[linear algebra]], and [[Tournament theory|theory of tournaments]].<ref name=tribute/>
